The factory closed on a Tuesday. No warning. No severance. Just a chain on the gate and a photocopied letter taped to the door. Three hundred workers showed up that morning expecting another shift. They got nothing. The town had depended on that plant for forty years. Now it was gone. Mayor Linda Cortez called an emergency meeting that night. The gymnasium was packed. People were angry. They were scared. One woman stood up and said she had three kids and no savings. Another man said he was two months from retirement. The company offered no explanation. Its executives were already on a plane to somewhere else. This is how it happens in small-town America. The jobs vanish. The promises evaporate. And the people left behind are expected to simply adapt. They always do. But it costs them something every time.
